claim: HT29-18N2 (N2) human colonic adenocarcinoma cells differentiate to goblet cells upon starvation in protein-free medium.
source: The human colonic adenocarcinoma cells HT29-18N2 (N2) differentiate to goblet cells upon starvation in protein-free medium (Phillips et al., 1995), which increases the production of MUC5AC.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Phillips et al., 1995, and is consistent with established knowledge about this cell line.

claim: Starvation in protein-free medium increases the production of MUC5AC in N2 cells.
source: The human colonic adenocarcinoma cells HT29-18N2 (N2) differentiate to goblet cells upon starvation in protein-free medium (Phillips et al., 1995), which increases the production of MUC5AC.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 1A), dot-blot quantification showing 45-fold increase (Figure 1B,C), and qRT-PCR data (Figure 1D).

claim: Starved N2 cells show a 45-fold increase of MUC5AC protein levels compared to nonstarved N2 cells.
source: Quantification of the dot blot revealed a 45-fold increase of MUC5AC protein levels in starved N2 cells compared to nonstarved N2 cells.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by quantification of dot blot data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: HeLa cells lack MUC5AC production.
source: Our findings with the dot-blot procedure confirm the lack of MUC5AC production in Hela cells (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by dot-blot analysis shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: MUC5AC mRNA levels are increased in starved N2 cells compared to nonstarved cells.
source: MUC5AC mRNA analysis by quantitative real-time PCR also confirmed increased MUC5AC mRNA levels in starved cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PMA treatment for 2 hours induces MUC5AC secretion from starved N2 goblet cells.
source: Starved goblet cells were treated for 2 hr with 2 µM PMA to induce MUC5AC secretion (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and chemiluminescence assay data in Figure 2B.

claim: PMA-induced MUC5AC secretion shows a significant increase at 15 min and maximal secretion at 2 hr post incubation with 2 µM PMA.
source: The time course for PMA induced MUC5AC secretion shows a significant increase at 15 min and maximal MUC5AC secretion is observed at 2 hr post incubation with 2 µM PMA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BAPTA-AM treatment severely inhibits PMA-stimulated MUC5AC secretion.
source: Depolymerization of actin filaments by Latrunculin A had no effect on PMA-stimulated MUC5AC secretion, while BAPTA-AM and the actin-stabilizing agent Jasplakinolide severely affected MUC5AC secretion (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemiluminescence assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Jasplakinolide treatment severely inhibits PMA-stimulated MUC5AC secretion.
source: Depolymerization of actin filaments by Latrunculin A had no effect on PMA-stimulated MUC5AC secretion, while BAPTA-AM and the actin-stabilizing agent Jasplakinolide severely affected MUC5AC secretion (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemiluminescence assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Latrunculin A treatment has no effect on PMA-stimulated MUC5AC secretion.
source: Depolymerization of actin filaments by Latrunculin A had no effect on PMA-stimulated MUC5AC secretion, while BAPTA-AM and the actin-stabilizing agent Jasplakinolide severely affected MUC5AC secretion (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemiluminescence assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ca2+ is required for PMA-dependent secretion of MUC5AC from starved N2 cells.
source: Inhibition of MUC5AC secretion by BAPTA-AM treatment confirms the known requirement of Ca2+ in the events leading to mucin secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by BAPTA-AM inhibition data in Figure 2C and is consistent with known mechanisms of mucin secretion.

claim: Actin filaments likely act as a barrier to prevent premature fusion of MUC5AC-containing granules with the cell surface.
source: The inhibitory effect of hyperstabilized actin filaments (by Jasplakinolide treatment) on MUC5AC secretion reveals that actin filaments likely act as a barrier to prevent premature fusion of MUC5AC-containing granules with the cell surface.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Jasplakinolide (which stabilizes actin) inhibits secretion while Latrunculin A (which depolymerizes actin) does not.

claim: BFA treatment causes Golgi membranes to fuse with the ER.
source: Befreldin A (BFA) is known to inhibit cargo export from the ER and causes Golgi membranes to fuse with the ER (Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 1989, and represents established knowledge.

claim: BFA treatment disperses GRASP65 in starved N2 cells.
source: The dispersal of GRASP65 with BFA treatment shows that our experimental conditions are effective in disrupting the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: BFA treatment does not affect MUC5AC staining in starved N2 cells.
source: However, MUC5AC staining was unperturbed by BFA treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: BFA severely inhibits the secretion of newly synthesized proteins from starved N2 cells.
source: Analysis of the medium revealed that BFA severely inhibited the secretion of newly synthesized proteins from the starved N2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BFA treatment does not affect PMA-dependent MUC5AC secretion.
source: The results reveal that BFA treatment does not affect PMA-dependent MUC5AC secretion under the experimental conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemiluminescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The mucin secretion assay measures only the secretion of MUC5AC contained in post-Golgi secretory carriers.
source: Therefore, in our assay, we only measure the secretion of MUC5AC contained in the post-Golgi secretory carriers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that BFA blocks ER-to-Golgi transport but does not affect PMA-induced MUC5AC secretion.

claim: The mucin secretion assay is independent of MUC5AC synthesis, export from the ER to the late Golgi, and its sorting and packing into the secretory granules.
source: This measurement is independent of MUC5AC synthesis, export from the ER to the late Golgi, and its sorting and packing into the secretory granules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BFA insensitivity of PMA-induced MUC5AC secretion.

claim: A screen of 7343 human gene products identified 413 components that upon knockdown resulted in hyposecretion of MUC5AC.
source: From this analysis we selected 413 components that upon knockdown resulted in hyposecretion and 534 that exhibited a hypersecretion of MUC5AC (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the screening data and analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: A screen of 7343 human gene products identified 534 components that upon knockdown resulted in hypersecretion of MUC5AC.
source: From this analysis we selected 413 components that upon knockdown resulted in hyposecretion and 534 that exhibited a hypersecretion of MUC5AC (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the screening data and analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: A validation screen confirmed 29 proteins that gave a MUC5AC hyposecretory phenotype.
source: A second validation screen with siRNAs distinct from the primary screen confirmed 29 proteins that gave a MUC5AC hyposecretory phenotype and 5 with a hypersecretory secretory defect (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the validation screen data described in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: A validation screen confirmed 5 proteins that gave a MUC5AC hypersecretory phenotype.
source: A second validation screen with siRNAs distinct from the primary screen confirmed 29 proteins that gave a MUC5AC hyposecretory phenotype and 5 with a hypersecretory secretory defect (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the validation screen data described in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: Depletion of individual PIMS does not affect general protein secretion in starved N2 cells.
source: We did not detect any obvious changes in the secreted polypeptide pool in starved N2 cells depleted of the individual PIMS compared with control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 16 of the 34 hits from the validation screen can be detected in N2 cells.
source: Our findings reveal that 16 of the 34 hits can be detected in N2 cells (Table 1 and Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A and summarized in Table 1.

claim: The mRNA levels of eight components remain unchanged upon starvation compared with unstarved cells.
source: Of these, the mRNA levels of eight components remain unchanged upon starvation compared with unstarved cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR quantification data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: In differentiated N2 cells the levels of GRIK4, KCNIP3, SIPA1, MAPK15, ATF6 and CCR9 are upregulated.
source: Interestingly, in differentiated N2 cells the levels of GRIK4, KCNIP3, SIPA1, MAPK15, ATF6 and CCR9 were upregulated, while the mRNA levels of SUR1 and SILV were downregulated (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR quantification data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: In differentiated N2 cells the mRNA levels of SUR1 and SILV are downregulated.
source: Interestingly, in differentiated N2 cells the levels of GRIK4, KCNIP3, SIPA1, MAPK15, ATF6 and CCR9 were upregulated, while the mRNA levels of SUR1 and SILV were downregulated (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR quantification data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: MUC5AC mRNA is upregulated upon starvation.
source: As expected, the MUC5AC mRNA was upregulated upon starvation whereas the mRNA levels for the housekeeping gene GAPDH remained unchanged (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR quantification data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: GAPDH mRNA levels remain unchanged upon starvation.
source: As expected, the MUC5AC mRNA was upregulated upon starvation whereas the mRNA levels for the housekeeping gene GAPDH remained unchanged (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR quantification data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: TRPM5 is required for the regulated secretion of insulin.
source: TRPM5, a hit in our assay, is required for the regulated secretion of insulin (Brixel et al., 2010; Colsoul et al., 2010) and this prompted us to further test its involvement in the regulated secretion of MUC5AC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brixel et al., 2010 and Colsoul et al., 2010.

claim: Stable knockdown of TRPM5 results in greater than 80% reduction in TRPM5 mRNA levels.
source: This procedure resulted in greater than 80% reduction in the TRPM5 mRNA levels (Figure 5A) and a 50% reduction in the quantity of PMA dependent MUC5AC secreted by starved cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative real-time PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Stable knockdown of TRPM5 results in a 50% reduction in PMA-dependent MUC5AC secretion.
source: This procedure resulted in greater than 80% reduction in the TRPM5 mRNA levels (Figure 5A) and a 50% reduction in the quantity of PMA dependent MUC5AC secreted by starved cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemiluminescence assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TRPM5 knockdown does not affect total MUC5AC protein levels in starved N2 cells.
source: The dot blot was quantified and revealed no difference in the total MUC5AC contents in the TRPM5 knockdown cells compared with control cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by dot blot quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Secretory granules are formed in TRPM5-depleted cells upon starvation.
source: GFP-positive cells indicate the expression of TRPM5 shRNA and show that secretory granules were formed in TRPM5-depleted cells upon starvation (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HA-TRPM5 localizes to the apical surface of polarized non-starved and starved N2 cells.
source: HA-TRPM5 was localized to the apical surface of the polarized non-starved and starved N2 cells while apical MUC5AC staining was only evident in starved N2 cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Apical MUC5AC staining is only evident in starved N2 cells.
source: HA-TRPM5 was localized to the apical surface of the polarized non-starved and starved N2 cells while apical MUC5AC staining was only evident in starved N2 cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Dialyzing N2 cells with 1 μM Ca2+ in the pipette solution generates an outwardly rectifying TRPM5-like current.
source: Dialyzing N2 cells with Ca2+-free intracellular pipette solutions resulted in negligibly low cationic current recorded; the presence of 1 μM Ca2+ in the pipette solution generated an outwardly rectifying TRPM5-like current (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Replacement of extracellular Na+ by N-methyl-D-glucamine reduces the inward current without affecting the outward current in N2 cells.
source: Replacement of extracellular Na+ by the non-permeant cation N-methyl-D-glucamine reduced the inward current without affecting the outward current (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of TRPM5 abolishes Ca2+-dependent cationic currents in starved N2 cells.
source: shRNA-mediated knockdown of TRPM5 abolished Ca2+-dependent cationic currents recorded in starved N2 cells (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: TRPM5 channel participates in the generation of the plasma membrane, nonselective, Ca2+-dependent cationic current in N2 cells.
source: Together, these results are consistent with the participation of the TRPM5 channel in the generation of the plasma membrane, nonselective, Ca2+-dependent cationic current in N2 cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the electrophysiology data showing Ca2+-dependent currents that are abolished by TRPM5 knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of TRPM5 significantly reduces ATP-induced secretion of MUC5AC.
source: Knockdown of TRPM5 significantly reduced ATP-induced secretion of MUC5AC (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by dot blot quantification data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: N2 cells cultured without Ca2+ in the extracellular medium do not secrete MUC5AC upon exposure to ATP.
source: N2 cells cultured without Ca2+ in the extracellular medium did not secrete MUC5AC upon exposure to ATP.
evidence: The claim is supported by dot blot quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There is a sixfold increase in MUC5AC secretion by differentiated N2 cells in the presence of extracellular Ca2+ upon ATP exposure.
source: However, there was a sixfold increase in MUC5AC secretion by differentiated N2 cells in the presence of extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dot blot quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: MUC5AC secretion by ionomycin is significantly higher than treatment with thapsigargin.
source: MUC5AC secretion by ionomycin was significantly higher than treatment with thapsigargin, however, these reagents were less effective, compared with ATP, in eliciting MUC5AC secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by dot blot quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The contribution of Ca2+ release from internal stores is not as significant as Ca2+ entry from the extracellular medium for MUC5AC secretion by N2 cells.
source: Together, these results indicate that the contribution of Ca2+ release from internal stores is not as significant as Ca2+ entry from the extracellular medium for MUC5AC secretion by N2 cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the effects of thapsigargin (ER Ca2+ release) versus ionomycin (extracellular Ca2+ entry) and the requirement for extracellular Ca2+ in ATP-induced secretion.

claim: ATP treatment elicits an increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration in starved N2 cells.
source: Consistent with the secretion data, measurements of intracellular Ca2+ levels in starved N2 cells loaded with the calcium dye Fura-2 showed that cells treated with ATP elicited an increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration, which was markedly decreased when extracellular Ca2+ was removed (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: ATP-induced increase in intracellular Ca2+ is markedly decreased when extracellular Ca2+ is removed.
source: Consistent with the secretion data, measurements of intracellular Ca2+ levels in starved N2 cells loaded with the calcium dye Fura-2 showed that cells treated with ATP elicited an increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration, which was markedly decreased when extracellular Ca2+ was removed (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: TRPM5-depleted cells show reduced increase in intracellular [Ca2+] after ATP treatment compared with control cells.
source: After ATP treatment, cells depleted of TRPM5 showed reduced increase in intracellular [Ca2+] compared with control cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In the absence of extracellular Ca2+ there is no difference between control and TRPM5 depleted cells in ATP-induced increase of intracellular Ca2+ levels.
source: In the absence of extracellular Ca2+ there was no difference between control and TRPM5 depleted cells in ATP-induced increase of intracellular Ca2+ levels, suggesting that TRPM5 participation in ATP-mediated MUC5AC secretion is related to the regulation of the secretagogue-induced Ca2+ entry.
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: TRPM5 participation in ATP-mediated MUC5AC secretion is related to the regulation of secretagogue-induced Ca2+ entry.
source: In the absence of extracellular Ca2+ there was no difference between control and TRPM5 depleted cells in ATP-induced increase of intracellular Ca2+ levels, suggesting that TRPM5 participation in ATP-mediated MUC5AC secretion is related to the regulation of the secretagogue-induced Ca2+ entry.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TRPM5 depletion only affects Ca2+ signals when extracellular Ca2+ is present.

claim: Starved N2 cells do not exhibit voltage-gated whole-cell Ca2+ currents.
source: However, we detected neither voltage-gated whole-cell Ca2+ currents (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A) nor depolarization-induced Ca2+ signals (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B) in starved N2 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Starved N2 cells do not exhibit depolarization-induced Ca2+ signals.
source: However, we detected neither voltage-gated whole-cell Ca2+ currents (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A) nor depolarization-induced Ca2+ signals (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B) in starved N2 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibitors of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels do not modify ATP-mediated Ca2+ signals in starved N2 cells.
source: Accordingly, inhibitors of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels did not modify ATP-mediated Ca2+ signals (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TRPM5-mediated Na+ entry is coupled to the functioning of a Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) in reverse mode, thereby promoting further Ca2+ entry.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that TRPM5-mediated Na+ entry was coupled to the functioning of a Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) in reverse mode, thereby promoting further Ca2+ entry.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the absence of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and is tested with NCX inhibitor experiments.

claim: ATP-induced MUC5AC secretion is greatly reduced in the presence of the NCX inhibitor KB-R9743.
source: ATP induced MUC5AC secretion was greatly reduced in the presence of the NCX inhibitor (Figure 9A), which suggests that TRPM5- and Ca2+-dependent MUC5AC secretion involves the activity of an NCX.
evidence: The claim is supported by dot blot quantification data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: TRPM5- and Ca2+-dependent MUC5AC secretion involves the activity of an NCX.
source: ATP induced MUC5AC secretion was greatly reduced in the presence of the NCX inhibitor (Figure 9A), which suggests that TRPM5- and Ca2+-dependent MUC5AC secretion involves the activity of an NCX.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NCX inhibitor reduces ATP-induced MUC5AC secretion.

claim: ATP-induced Ca2+ signals are reduced by approximately 50% in cells treated with the NCX inhibitor.
source: ATP-induced Ca2+ signals were reduced by ∼ 50% in cells treated with the NCX inhibitor (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: In the presence of the NCX inhibitor there is no difference in Ca2+ signals between control and TRPM5-depleted N2 cells.
source: Similar to the results obtained in the absence of extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 8D), in the presence of the NCX inhibitor there was no difference in Ca2+ signals between control and TRPM5-depleted N2 cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: N2 cells exhibit an ATP-induced Ca2+ entry mechanism that is consistent with the operation of an NCX in reverse mode.
source: These results suggest that N2 cells exhibit an ATP-induced Ca2+ entry mechanism that is consistent with the operation of an NCX in reverse mode and this control mechanism is lost in N2 cells depleted of TRPM5.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations that NCX inhibitor reduces Ca2+ entry and eliminates the difference between control and TRPM5-depleted cells.

claim: The ATP-induced Ca2+ entry control mechanism is lost in N2 cells depleted of TRPM5.
source: These results suggest that N2 cells exhibit an ATP-induced Ca2+ entry mechanism that is consistent with the operation of an NCX in reverse mode and this control mechanism is lost in N2 cells depleted of TRPM5.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NCX inhibitor eliminates the difference between control and TRPM5-depleted cells.

claim: MUC5AC is secreted by goblet cells of the respiratory tract.
source: The secreted gel-forming mucins MUC2, MUC5AC, MUC5B and MUC6 are produced by goblet cells, which are present in the epithelia and submucosal glands of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tract (Thornton et al., 2008; McGuckin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thornton et al., 2008 and McGuckin et al., 2011, and represents established knowledge.

claim: Human colon cancer expresses MUC5AC de novo.
source: Surprisingly, human pathologies such as colon cancer and ulcerative colitis produce MUC5AC de novo, which is then secreted (Bartman et al., 1999; Kocer et al., 2002; Forgue-Lafitte et al., 2007; Bu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Ulcerative colitis produces MUC5AC de novo.
source: Surprisingly, human pathologies such as colon cancer and ulcerative colitis produce MUC5AC de novo, which is then secreted (Bartman et al., 1999; Kocer et al., 2002; Forgue-Lafitte et al., 2007; Bu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: In cells of the gastro-intestinal lining, influx of extracellular Ca2+ participates in the release of mucins from the secretory granules.
source: In cells of the gastro-intestinal lining (Bou-Hanna et al., 1994; Barcelo et al., 2001; Bertrand et al., 2004) and eye conjunctiva (Li et al., 2012) influx of extracellular Ca2+ participates in the release of mucins from the secretory granules.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: In eye conjunctiva cells, influx of extracellular Ca2+ participates in the release of mucins from the secretory granules.
source: In cells of the gastro-intestinal lining (Bou-Hanna et al., 1994; Barcelo et al., 2001; Bertrand et al., 2004) and eye conjunctiva (Li et al., 2012) influx of extracellular Ca2+ participates in the release of mucins from the secretory granules.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: Extracellular Ca2+ is required for mucin secretion from cholinergic stimulated swine airway submucosal glands.
source: However, extracellular Ca2+ is required for mucin secretion from cholinergic stimulated swine airway submucosal glands (Lu et al., 2011) as well as by cold and menthol stimulated human bronchial epithelial cells (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2011.

claim: Extracellular Ca2+ is required for mucin secretion by cold and menthol stimulated human bronchial epithelial cells.
source: However, extracellular Ca2+ is required for mucin secretion from cholinergic stimulated swine airway submucosal glands (Lu et al., 2011) as well as by cold and menthol stimulated human bronchial epithelial cells (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: The involvement of extracellular Ca2+ in mucin secretion is likely to be cell type, signal, and mucin specific.
source: The involvement of extracellular Ca2+ in mucin secretion is therefore likely to be cell type, signal, and mucin specific.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that different cell types and stimuli show different requirements for extracellular Ca2+.

claim: Overproduction and hyper secretion of gel-forming mucins is linked to COPD, asthma and cystic fibrosis.
source: Overproduction and hyper secretion of gel-forming mucins is linked to COPD, asthma and cystic fibrosis (Rose and Voynow, 2006) and to the protection of the gut lining against infection and growth of a number of parasites including H. pylori.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rose and Voynow, 2006, and represents established knowledge.

claim: Inhibition of synthesis and secretion of mucins is linked to inflammatory bowel diseases such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.
source: Inhibition of synthesis and secretion of mucins is linked to inflammatory bowel diseases such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease (Corfield et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Corfield et al., 2001, and represents established knowledge.

claim: The functional coupling between endogenous TRPM5 channel and NCX has not been previously reported.
source: However, our observation describes for the first time the functional coupling between endogenous TRPM5 channel and NCX, and its physiological relevance in the context of mucin secretion.
evidence: The claim is based on the novelty of the findings presented in this manuscript.

claim: The functional coupling between TRPM5 and NCX is physiologically relevant in the context of mucin secretion.
source: However, our observation describes for the first time the functional coupling between endogenous TRPM5 channel and NCX, and its physiological relevance in the context of mucin secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing that both TRPM5 and NCX are required for ATP-induced MUC5AC secretion.

claim: TRPM5 activation by ATP couples TRPM5-mediated Na+ entry to promote Ca2+ uptake via an NCX to trigger MUC5AC secretion.
source: Thus TRPM5 activation by ATP couples TRPM5-mediated Na+ entry to promote Ca2+ uptake via an NCX to trigger MUC5AC secretion.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the experimental findings showing that TRPM5 is required for ATP-induced Ca2+ entry, which depends on NCX activity.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of 7343 human gene products in HT29-18N2 cells revealed new proteins for MUC5AC secretion.
source: siRNA-mediated knockdown of 7343 human gene products in a human colonic cancer goblet cell line (HT29-18N2) revealed new proteins, including a Ca2+-activated channel TRPM5, for MUC5AC secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by the screening data and validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: TRPM5 was required for PMA-induced secretion of MUC5AC from post-Golgi secretory granules.
source: TRPM5 was required for PMA and ATP-induced secretion of MUC5AC from the post-Golgi secretory granules.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that TRPM5 knockdown reduces PMA-induced secretion and that this secretion is BFA-insensitive.

claim: TRPM5 was required for ATP-induced secretion of MUC5AC from post-Golgi secretory granules.
source: TRPM5 was required for PMA and ATP-induced secretion of MUC5AC from the post-Golgi secretory granules.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that TRPM5 knockdown reduces ATP-induced secretion and that this secretion is BFA-insensitive.

claim: Stable knockdown of TRPM5 reduced a TRPM5-like current.
source: Stable knockdown of TRPM5 reduced a TRPM5-like current and ATP-mediated Ca2+ signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Stable knockdown of TRPM5 reduced ATP-mediated Ca2+ signal.
source: Stable knockdown of TRPM5 reduced a TRPM5-like current and ATP-mediated Ca2+ signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: ATP-induced MUC5AC secretion depends strongly on Ca2+ influx.
source: ATP-induced MUC5AC secretion depended strongly on Ca2+ influx, which was markedly reduced in TRPM5 knockdown cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that ATP-induced secretion is abolished in the absence of extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 7B).

claim: Ca2+ influx is markedly reduced in TRPM5 knockdown cells.
source: ATP-induced MUC5AC secretion depended strongly on Ca2+ influx, which was markedly reduced in TRPM5 knockdown cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The difference in ATP-induced Ca2+ entry between control and TRPM5 knockdown cells is abrogated in the absence of extracellular Ca2+.
source: The difference in ATP-induced Ca2+ entry between control and TRPM5 knockdown cells was abrogated in the absence of extracellular Ca2+ and by inhibition of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The difference in ATP-induced Ca2+ entry between control and TRPM5 knockdown cells is abrogated by inhibition of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX).
source: The difference in ATP-induced Ca2+ entry between control and TRPM5 knockdown cells was abrogated in the absence of extracellular Ca2+ and by inhibition of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX).
evidence: The claim is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: MUC5AC secretion is reduced by inhibition of NCX.
source: Accordingly, MUC5AC secretion was reduced by inhibition of NCX.
evidence: The claim is supported by dot blot quantification data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: MUC5AC is one of the major components of the mucus in the airways.
source: The secretory or gel-forming mucin, Mucin 5AC (MUC5AC) is one of the major components of the mucus in the airways, and hyper- or hyposecretion of this component is a hallmark of a number of chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases (COPD) (Rose and Voynow, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rose and Voynow, 2006, and represents established knowledge.

claim: Hyper- or hyposecretion of MUC5AC is a hallmark of chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases (COPD).
source: The secretory or gel-forming mucin, Mucin 5AC (MUC5AC) is one of the major components of the mucus in the airways, and hyper- or hyposecretion of this component is a hallmark of a number of chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases (COPD) (Rose and Voynow, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rose and Voynow, 2006, and represents established knowledge.

claim: MUC5AC is expressed at low levels in the gastrointestinal tract.
source: MUC5AC is also expressed at low levels in the gastrointestinal tract and, surprisingly, expressed de novo, and upregulated in colonic mucus from cancer and ulcerative colitis patients (Bartman et al., 1999; Kocer et al., 2002; Byrd and Bresalier, 2004; Forgue-Lafitte et al., 2007; Bu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: MUC5AC is expressed de novo and upregulated in colonic mucus from cancer patients.
source: MUC5AC is also expressed at low levels in the gastrointestinal tract and, surprisingly, expressed de novo, and upregulated in colonic mucus from cancer and ulcerative colitis patients (Bartman et al., 1999; Kocer et al., 2002; Byrd and Bresalier, 2004; Forgue-Lafitte et al., 2007; Bu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: MUC5AC is expressed de novo and upregulated in colonic mucus from ulcerative colitis patients.
source: MUC5AC is also expressed at low levels in the gastrointestinal tract and, surprisingly, expressed de novo, and upregulated in colonic mucus from cancer and ulcerative colitis patients (Bartman et al., 1999; Kocer et al., 2002; Byrd and Bresalier, 2004; Forgue-Lafitte et al., 2007; Bu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: MUC5AC is expressed in response to parasitic infection.
source: MUC5AC is also expressed in response to parasitic infection, which is probably its additional physiological role (Hasnain et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hasnain et al., 2011.

claim: The apparent molecular weight of MUC5AC increases from 500 kD of monomeric unglycosylated ER form to 2.2 MD by glycosylation and oligomerization during its transit through the Golgi apparatus.
source: The apparent molecular weight of the gel-forming MUC5AC increases from 500 kD of monomeric unglycosylated ER form (van Klinken et al., 1998) to 2.2 MD (Thornton et al., 1996) by glycosylation and oligomerization during its transit through the Golgi apparatus to a secreted form that reaches up to 40 MD in apparent molecular weight (Sheehan et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to van Klinken et al., 1998 and Thornton et al., 1996, and represents established knowledge.

claim: Secreted MUC5AC reaches up to 40 MD in apparent molecular weight.
source: The apparent molecular weight of the gel-forming MUC5AC increases from 500 kD of monomeric unglycosylated ER form (van Klinken et al., 1998) to 2.2 MD (Thornton et al., 1996) by glycosylation and oligomerization during its transit through the Golgi apparatus to a secreted form that reaches up to 40 MD in apparent molecular weight (Sheehan et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sheehan et al., 2000, and represents established knowledge.

claim: Condensed mucins expand their volume up to 1000-fold upon secretion.
source: The MSG fuse with the plasma membrane, in a signal-dependent manner, and the condensed mucins expand their volume up to 1000-fold upon secretion (Verdugo, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Verdugo, 1993, and represents established knowledge.

claim: The signaling events that lead to mucin secretion in the airways involve mainly P2Y purinergic and muscarinic receptor activation by ATP and acetylcholine, respectively.
source: The signaling events that lead to mucin secretion in the airways involve mainly, but not exclusively, P2Y purinergic and muscarinic receptor activation by ATP and acetylcholine, respectively.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about mucin secretion signaling.

claim: P2Y purinergic and muscarinic receptor activation generates diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1, 4, 5-triphosphate (IP3).
source: The subsequent generation of diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1, 4, 5-triphosphate (IP3) activate protein kinase-C (PKC) and cause the release of Ca2+ from the ER to promote mucus secretion (Bou-Hanna et al., 1994; Abdullah et al., 1996, 1997; Bertrand et al., 2004; Ehre et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge about mucin secretion signaling.
